learningObjective: Decide whether ordinary cross-validation answers the deployment question, and choose a structure-aware split, external evaluation, representative holdout, or nested evaluation when it does not.
mediumRationale: A compact semantic decision sequence is the smallest medium that separates two often-confused questions: whether folds preserve the unit that must be unseen, and whether cross-validation measures the target deployment distribution at all. Ordered checks connect each failed assumption to its replacement without implying that one split is universally correct, and remain legible without horizontal scrolling at 390 CSS pixels.

pages.insight: The preceding slide recommends regularization and validation-loss early stopping but does not discuss fold construction, deployment shift, grouped observations, or temporal ordering.

The deck's only explicit cross-validation guidance says to use cross-validation to determine hyperparameters before ensembling; it does not distinguish tuning from unbiased evaluation or identify cases where ordinary random folds answer the wrong question.

sourceReview.notes: The hardest prose-only mental model is that cross-validation is useful only after the evaluation target and split boundary match deployment. Structure-aware folds can prevent future, group, or spatial leakage, but they still estimate performance on the sampled distribution; they cannot substitute for a deployment sample or online experiment under shift. Separately, when cross-validation scores drive hyperparameter selection, an untouched outer loop or final test is needed for honest evaluation. The visual makes these constraints sequential and makes no empirical performance claim.

implementation.accessibility: The figure has a linked learning objective and an explicitly labelled semantic group. Four ordered checks name both the failed assumption and replacement evaluation, so no inference relies on color. The sequence uses ordinary wrapping text with no fixed width or horizontal scrolling at 390 CSS pixels; established theme tokens support dark mode, and existing print rules provide a light high-contrast rendering and keep the caption with the figure.
